advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] In run_gc, return skipped="locked" only when lock_kernel.is_contention(exc) is true, and re-raise any other OSError
evidence: src/rebar/_store/lock_kernel.py:123-124: "Raises :class:`OSError` if the lock could not be taken — pass it to :func:`is_contention` to tell \"someone else holds it\" from a real fault"

src/rebar/_store/lock_kernel.py:185-189: is_contention "False for every other errno — those are real faults (ENOLCK/EIO/EBADF/…) that must surface with their identity rather than be waited out as contention."
src/rebar/_store/lock_kernel.py:132: the Windows leg also calls os.lseek before msvcrt.locking, so lseek failures fall into the same catch-all
advisory.finding: run_gc maps every OSError from lock_kernel.take_exclusive to GcResult(skipped="locked"). A real lock fault (EBADF, ENOLCK, EIO, or a failing os.lseek or msvcrt.locking on the new Windows path) looks exactly like another GC pass holding the lock, so GC can silently never run. lock_kernel provides is_contention to tell the two apart.
scenarios: On Windows, msvcrt.locking fails with an errno outside the contention set. Every run_gc call then returns skipped="locked", the store is never reclaimed, and nothing reports why.
On POSIX, ENOLCK on a network filesystem looks like a permanently busy GC interlock.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Move `_unlink_git_object` into one shared test helper module and import it in the three test files
advisory.finding: The same `_unlink_git_object` helper (chmod to S_IWRITE|S_IREAD, then unlink, with a missing_ok branch) is copied verbatim into three test modules. Two of those modules never pass missing_ok, and a fourth module reimplements the same chmod-retry idea.
scenarios: A later fix to the Windows read-only-object workaround is applied in one copy but not the others, and the sweep regresses in only some modules.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Make test_gc_lock_is_exclusive (and the gc_trigger overlap test) hold the lock with lock_kernel.take_exclusive instead of fcntl.flock, and drop the fcntl-only skipif, so the msvcrt contention path runs in the Windows sweep
evidence: tests/unit/test_snapshot_janitor.py:222: @pytest.mark.skipif(fcntl is None, reason="POSIX flock required")

Diff adds to src/rebar/_snapshot/janitor.py: `+            lock_kernel.take_exclusive(fd)` / `+        except OSError:` / `+            return GcResult(skipped="locked")` — the lines that now run on Windows
src/rebar/_store/lock_kernel.py:130-133: the msvcrt leg (`os.lseek(fd, 0, os.SEEK_SET)`; `msvcrt.locking(fd, msvcrt.LK_NBLCK, _WINDOWS_LOCK_BYTES)`) is what run_gc reaches on Windows
advisory.finding: run_gc's new Windows lock path (lock_kernel.take_exclusive → msvcrt LK_NBLCK → `except OSError: return GcResult(skipped="locked")`) has no test that runs on Windows. Both tests that hold the GC lock and assert the 'locked' skip are marked `skipif(fcntl is None)` and hold the lock through fcntl.flock directly. So in the Windows sweep this diff targets, a broken msvcrt contention path (wrong errno, missing lseek anchor, or a second pass running alongside the first) would go unnoticed.
scenarios: Windows sweep: a second run_gc starts while a first one holds gc/lock. The test that should check it returns skipped="locked" is skipped, so overlapping GC passes (AC7) would not be caught.
advisory.suggested_fix: In test_gc_lock_is_exclusive replace `fcntl.flock(held, fcntl.LOCK_EX)` / `fcntl.flock(held, fcntl.LOCK_UN)` with `lock_kernel.take_exclusive(held)` / `lock_kernel.release_exclusive(held)` and remove `@pytest.mark.skipif(fcntl is None, ...)`. Windows byte-range locks are per handle, so a second os.open handle in the same process is still refused. Do the same in test_overlap_with_a_concurrent_run_gc_stands_aside_and_keeps_the_clock.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] In the Windows branch, drive janitor._evict(store, dest) while the reader holds the fd, and assert it returns 0, dest still exists, and fh still reads the content, instead of asserting a raw os.rename raises
evidence: tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py:160-162: "# Windows refuses to rename a directory holding an open file. The janitor's / # _evict treats that OSError as \"nothing reclaimed\" and keeps the entry, so / # the live reader is protected by the refusal instead of by delete-on-close."
tests/unit/test_snapshot_cache.py:163-164: `with pytest.raises(PermissionError):` / `os.rename(dest, trash)` — asserts OS behavior, not the unit's
src/rebar/_snapshot/janitor.py:207-210: `try: os.rename(entry, dest)` / `except OSError:` / `return 0` — the contract the comment relies on, not called by the test
advisory.finding: The new Windows branch of test_open_reader_survives_eviction_then_relookup_misses only checks that the OS refuses a raw `os.rename` of a directory holding an open file. Its comment says the live reader is protected because 'the janitor's _evict treats that OSError as "nothing reclaimed" and keeps the entry', but the test never calls janitor._evict or run_gc. The janitor behavior that protects the reader is not exercised: no return of 0, entry still present, no sidecar removal, no add_bytes decrement. If _evict were changed to, say, fall back to an in-place rmtree after the rename fails, this test would still pass.
scenarios: A later change makes _evict fall back to shutil.rmtree(entry) when the rename is refused. On Windows that deletes a live reader's entry or decrements the byte total, and the Windows branch stays green because it only exercises os.rename.
advisory.suggested_fix: Replace the `with pytest.raises(PermissionError): os.rename(dest, trash)` block with `assert janitor._evict(store, dest) == 0; assert dest.exists(); assert fh.read() == b"content\n"`. After fh.close(), call `janitor._evict(store, dest)` again and assert it returns a positive size before the re-lookup assertions.
